did_you_know.text: Did you know? After Nahash, king of the Ammonites, died, his son Hanun became king. David wanted to maintain a relationship of kindness with the house of Nahash, so he sent a delegation to express his condolences.
Did you know? The Ammonite officials interpreted David’s delegation as an act of espionage. They claimed that the messengers had been sent to investigate the city, spy on it, and overthrow it.

Did you know? Hanun humiliated David’s messengers in two ways: he shaved off half of each man’s beard and cut their garments off at the waist. Thus, an attempt to comfort the king became an act that led to a military conflict.

Did you know? David did not immediately send the messengers back to Jerusalem. Instead, he instructed them to remain in Jericho until their beards grew back and they could return. The text emphasizes that they were deeply ashamed.

Did you know? After realizing that they had damaged their relationship with David, the Ammonites hired armies from Aram-beth-rehob, Aram-zobah, Maacah, and Tob. According to the text, the hired forces numbered tens of thousands of soldiers.

Did you know? Joab faced a situation in which the enemy surrounded Israel from two directions: the Arameans stood in the open field behind him, while the Ammonites positioned themselves in front of the city. So he divided his army into two units.

Did you know? Joab and Abishai agreed on a principle of mutual support: if either of them faced difficulty against the enemy, the other would come to his aid. In this way, they confronted the danger of fighting on two fronts.

Did you know? Joab’s words did not end with a military plan but with a statement of faith. He called them to be strong for the sake of the people and the cities of God, adding that the Lord would do what seemed good to him.
Did you know? After Joab defeated Aram, the Arameans did not give up but regrouped. Hadadezer sent forces from Aram beyond the Euphrates, commanded by Shobach, the commander of his army.

Did you know? At the end of the campaign, the kings of Aram who had been subject to Hadadezer saw that they had been defeated by Israel, made peace with Israel, and became subject to them. As a result, the Arameans stopped helping the Ammonites.
